strengths: Clear identification and systematic empirical documentation of SFT plateau across 6 data scales (200k-2.8M), providing concrete evidence for a practical limitation in chart-to-code generation
Substantial dataset contribution: 3M-pair training corpus using real-world tables from arXiv, larger and more realistic than prior purely synthetic datasets
Strong empirical results achieving SOTA among open-source MLLMs (96.5% execution rate, 83.8% high-level score on ChartMimic) with consistent improvements across benchmarks (6.2-9.9% gains)
Competitive with GPT-4o on multiple metrics (Table 2): exceeds GPT-4o on text, layout, and type dimensions despite using 7B vs. much larger proprietary model

Comprehensive experimental validation with thorough ablations examining SFT vs. RL (Table 3), reward components (Table 4), and two-stage design (Table 5), plus training curves illustrating component contributions

Thoughtfully designed multi-granularity reward system addressing practical issues: code normalization for handling syntactic diversity, render-and-compare for visual fidelity, rule-based textual validation across five dimensions
Clear presentation with informative pipeline diagrams (Figure 2) and qualitative examples (Figure 5) demonstrating visual fidelity improvements over baselines
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Individual components are well-established (RLVR from Shao et al. 2024, standard MLLM visual evaluation, GRPO from prior work). Primary contribution is engineering-focused combination rather than fundamental algorithmic innovation

Dataset claims of moving beyond synthetic data are overstated: While tables are from arXiv, plotting code is generated by Gemini-2.5-Flash. Missing analysis of code quality, programming style diversity, and actual distribution compared to real plotting code

SFT plateau analysis lacks depth: No investigation of whether larger models (13B, 34B) avoid plateau, making unclear if this is fundamental limitation or model-capacity issue. Limited analysis of which chart types saturate first or specific failure modes

Circular visual reward dependency: Uses larger Qwen2.5-VL-72B model to evaluate outputs from smaller Qwen2.5-VL-7B, potentially biasing the reward signal. No validation that visual rewards correlate with ground-truth fidelity

Evaluation clarity issues: Zero-shot setting raises questions about data source disjointness with training set (not explicitly clarified). ReachQA evaluation uses only 500 samples. No confidence intervals or statistical significance testing reported

Critical missing comparisons: Recent concurrent works (Chart-R1, BigCharts-R1, Point-RFT) mentioned but not compared quantitatively despite using similar RL approaches, limiting understanding of relative contributions

Reproducibility gaps: Dataset not stated as released. Significant computational overhead (60 hrs SFT + 34 hrs RL on 24 H800 GPUs) without cost analysis. Visual reward computation overhead unknown. Hyperparameter choices (e.g., wt=0.5, wv=0.5) lack justification

Weak two-stage training justification: Table 5 shows only marginal performance differences (83.83% vs. 82.61%), leaving unclear why textual→visual is superior to alternatives. Motivation for this specific curriculum not well explained
Generalization concerns: Narrow scope (single task), tested only on one base model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B). No evidence of broader applicability to other structured output tasks or architectures
Insufficient error analysis: No systematic discussion of failure modes, chart types where MSRL struggles, or behavior when code fails to render despite this being mentioned as occurring

strengths: Systematic demonstration of SFT plateau phenomenon through large-scale experiments at multiple data scales (200k to 2.8M samples), providing clear empirical motivation
Comprehensive and well-motivated multi-granularity reward design combining rule-based textual evaluation (5 dimensions) with VLM-based visual evaluation (6 dimensions)

Substantial dataset contribution: 3M chart-code pairs from real-world arXiv tables with realistic distributions, 24 chart types, 1,555 API types, exceeding prior synthetic datasets in scale and diversity

Strong empirical results achieving SOTA among open-source models with +6.2% and +9.9% improvements on ChartMimic and ReachQA benchmarks respectively, competitive with GPT-4o (much larger proprietary model)
Rigorous experimental validation with comprehensive ablations (Tables 4-6, Appendix C) examining SFT/RL contributions, reward types, visual evaluators, and optimizer choices (GRPO vs DPO)
Practical two-stage curriculum training strategy efficiently balances computational cost and performance gains (cheap textual rewards first, then expensive visual rewards on subset)
Good reproducibility with detailed implementation details, exact prompts in appendices, clear dataset construction methodology, and code release promised
Well-executed paper with clear presentation of methodology, thorough baseline comparisons across proprietary and open-source models, and systematic exploration of design space
weaknesses: Narrow scope limited to chart-to-code generation task; unclear whether insights and methods generalize to other structured output generation problems, limiting broader impact

Insufficient comparison with concurrent RL-based approaches for chart generation (Chart-R1, BigCharts-R1 mentioned but not directly compared), making it unclear what advantages MSRL offers over simpler RL baselines

Visual reward validation concerns: consistency check limited to 100 samples with 90% agreement; potential overfitting to Qwen2.5-VL-72B evaluator preferences; no analysis of reward correlation with downstream task performance

Computational cost not fully justified: ~94 GPU-hours total training cost (60h SFT + 34h RL on 24 H800 GPUs); no comparison showing whether +6.2% improvement justifies this overhead vs. other efficiency approaches

Dataset generated by LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4.1-mini) rather than human-annotated; potential bias in code patterns, style, and complexity; no analysis of distribution shift or inherited LLM failure modes
Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multi-run variance estimates; modest stage-2 improvements (+1.5%, Figure 4) lack significance testing

Hyperparameter choices appear somewhat arbitrary (reward weights, two-stage architecture) with limited justification; no ablation on weight selection or exploration of alternative curriculum strategies

Limited failure analysis: qualitative examples show remaining issues (spurious titles, layout errors) but no systematic error categorization by chart type; generalization tests use only 107-150 samples each (Seaborn, Plotly)

Methodological concerns: two-stage training is pragmatic but ad-hoc; no formal analysis of multi-objective optimization or convergence criteria; convergence claims based on visual inspection of Figure 4

Some key details relegated to appendices; connection to broader curriculum learning and multi-objective RL literature could be strengthened; incomplete discussion of which aspects are task-specific vs. generalizable

strengths: Systematic empirical analysis of SFT plateau with multi-scale experiments (200k-2.8M), providing valuable documentation of scaling behavior
Large-scale chart-to-code dataset (3M pairs) curated from real-world arXiv tables, addressing limitations of prior synthetic datasets and enabling reproducible plateau analysis

Strong empirical results achieving SOTA among open-source models (96.5% execution rate, 83.8 high-level score on ChartMimic) with comprehensive ablations examining SFT/RL interactions, reward components, and algorithm choices
Multi-granularity reward design combining rule-based textual validation with MLLM-based visual evaluation is well-motivated for structured output generation
Excellent reproducibility support including detailed implementation details, exact hyperparameters, prompts, training procedures, and code in supplementary materials
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and well-structured narrative communicating the core contributions
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: textual rewards use standard rule-based code evaluation, visual rewards via MLLM evaluation are becoming routine, GRPO algorithm is from prior work (Shao et al. 2024), and two-stage curriculum reflects engineering practicality rather than methodological innovation

Critical inconsistency in dataset narrative: 3M dataset claimed as main contribution but SFT plateaus around 2M, and functional RL dataset is only 33k samples after aggressive filtering, suggesting improvements may derive from careful curation rather than RL algorithm effectiveness

RL convergence analysis concerning: Figure 4 shows stage 1 converges at 22k samples and stage 2 at 11k—suspiciously small amounts that question whether RL truly 'breaks' the plateau or exploits curated data, with both stages reaching plateau rapidly

Overstated performance claims: comparison with GPT-4o is marginal and within noise given 600-example test set (78.6 vs 79.0 low-level, 83.8 vs 83.5 high-level), with paper claiming 'competitive' performance despite underperformance on both metrics

Evaluation limitations: no statistical significance testing despite small test sets (600 ChartMimic, 500 ReachQA examples); no confidence intervals; generalization tests on Seaborn/Plotly use only 107-150 samples with 15-20 point gaps between execution and high-level scores

Code normalization described as crucial for textual rewards but minimally detailed without ablation study; hyperparameter choices (wt, wv, we values) appear arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis; visual evaluator selection driven by computational cost rather than performance optimization

Heavy MLLM evaluation dependence: Appendix C shows results vary significantly with evaluator choice, GPT-4.1 correlates best with humans but main method uses Qwen2.5-VL-72B for cost reasons, raising reproducibility concerns; vision models in Table B perform poorly, indicating coarse-grained evaluation

Computational cost undermines practical utility: visual rewards require 1344 GPU hours vs 240 for textual-only (5.6× increase) for modest 1.5% additional gain, suggesting limited scalability and real-world applicability

Missing key comparisons: no empirical comparison with Chart-R1 or BigCharts-R1 (Chen et al. 2025a, Masry et al. 2025), which are directly relevant concurrent RL-based chart reasoning works cited but not evaluated against

Dataset reproducibility limited: 3M pairs require proprietary APIs (Gemini-2.5-Flash for generation, GPT-4.1 for visual filtering) with no mention of public release, constraining community access and reproducibility despite provided code

strengths: Systematic and rigorous empirical characterization of the SFT plateau across multiple data scales (200k-2.8M samples), providing valuable practical insight
Substantial dataset contribution: 3M chart-code pairs from real-world arXiv tables with 24 chart types and 1,555 APIs, significantly more realistic and diverse than prior synthetic datasets
Strong empirical results achieving SOTA among open-source models (83.8% high-level on ChartMimic) and competitive performance with GPT-4o despite 7x smaller model size
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including extensive ablations, multi-benchmark assessment, detailed low-level metrics, and out-of-domain generalization tests
Sensible multi-granularity reward design combining rule-based textual rewards (fine-grained code correctness) and model-based visual rewards (overall chart structure)
Exceptional reproducibility effort with detailed implementation details, exact prompts, hyperparameters, and supplementary code
Thorough documentation of data generation pipeline and filtering strategy with clear separation of SFT and RL datasets
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: MSRL combines existing techniques (GRPO, rule-based+model-based rewards, curriculum learning) in a straightforward manner without significant conceptual advances

Dataset quality concerns: all code generated by LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Flash) introducing potential biases; visual filtering relies on GPT-4.1-mini with only 100 manual verification samples; no human evaluation of code correctness across full dataset; potential copyright implications not addressed

RL evaluation limitations: very small RL dataset (33k, 1.2% of SFT) makes it difficult to isolate method effectiveness from data selection effects; multi-stage filtering introduces selection bias; expensive visual reward computation (72B model) limits reproducibility

SFT plateau analysis lacks depth: plateau could reflect distribution mismatch (LLM-generated→real charts) rather than pure data limits; no error categorization of plateau-region mistakes; alternative explanations insufficiently explored

Incomplete experimental validation: SFT baseline trained for only 1 epoch with fixed learning rate; modest out-of-domain generalization (257 samples) with 5-15% improvements; benchmark sizes relatively small (600, 500 samples); comparisons use 'updated' ChartCoder results due to flawed original evaluation

Mechanistic understanding gaps: limited analysis of what RL specifically learns beyond fine-grained details; no cost-benefit analysis of expensive visual reward computation; brief failure case analysis despite Figures E-F showing non-trivial errors

Reproducibility barriers: significant computational requirements (60+34 GPU-hours on H800s); reliance on 72B visual evaluator and specific rendering infrastructure; out-of-domain generalization demonstrated on tiny datasets

Generalization and scope limitations: model trained exclusively on Matplotlib; task-specific contributions; methodological insights limited to chart-to-code domain; 6.5% remaining gap to GPT-4o suggests substantial headroom
